Binarization The term ‘‘binarization’’ means to reduce a multi-value digital signal into a two-value binary signal ( Matsui & Mita, 1990 ). Among the global thresholding techniques for image binarization, Otsu’s method ( Otsu, 1975 ) is one of the best threshold selections. The basic idea of Otsu’s method is select an optimal threshold value to split grey-level histogram of an image into two parts based on the principle of maximum between-cluster variance and minimum within-cluster variance. The gray-level image in Fig. 3 was pro- cessed with Otsu’s method, and the segmentation results are shown in Fig. 4 . As expected, the green plants are identiﬁed and marked as white pixels. 2.2.3. The estimation of candidate center points Prior to the estimation of the position of crop rows, it is impor- tant to determine a number of center points indicating the centers of crop rows. It is directly related to the success or failure of the crop rows detection. In fact, the corresponding center points on two adjacent horizontal scanning lines cannot have a large devia- tion. In view of this, once the center points on some scan line were got, the remaining center points could be easily found based on the context information. Conclusions In this paper, an approach of robust recognition of crop rows based on multi-ROIs is presented. Firstly a original color image is transformed into a gray scale image. Then a binarization process is executed based on Otsu’s method, which provided the founda- tion for identifying green plants (crops and weeds). Considering the fact that the spacing between crop rows is equal, a model based on multi-ROIs, making an important contribution for estimating of points indicating the center lines of crop rows. A simple classiﬁca- tion method was applied to conﬁrm the real center points indicat- ing crop rows. Finally, the linear least square method is employed for calculating equations of straight lines corresponding to the crop rows. The proposed method can detect crop rows with all kinds of crop cultivated with rows even in the areas of the ﬁeld where patches of weed or bare patches occur. In addition, the method has a superior performance over SHT. However, the research on automatic crop rows detection has still a long way to go considering the complexity of the problem as a whole. Future work may be conducted in regard to three fac- ets. First, the color indices we used only has to highlight the green plants, but the effectiveness drops when the green spectral compo- nent becomes less important, thus the proposed approach should be extended to deal with other conditions. Second, the system should be designed with a more intelligent expert, so that combi- nation of all categorized algorithms would be appreciable, neural network for plant and weed classiﬁcation, machine vision for crop rows detection, fuzzy systems for obstacle avoidance and other techniques would be necessary ( Mousazadeh, 2013 ). Lastly, the fusion of vision sensor with other navigation sensors, such as Global Positioning System (GPS) and inertial sensor, to provide additional information to help with tasks such as end-of-row detection should be an active research topic in the future. Moreover, this approach was computationally demanding ( Leemans & Destain, 2006 ). (4) Methods based on stereovision: Stereovision also has been used successfully to detect crop rows. For example, Kise, Zhang, and Rovira Más (2005) used stereo images to analyze the geometry of ﬁeld terrain to detect crop rows. Wang, Zhang, Rovira-Más, and Tian (2011) developed a stereo image-processing algorithm to detect and track ground features. These features were used as reference points to calculate the lateral offset. Field validation tests showed that this algorithm could provide accurate relative lateral offset measurements. However, this approach was based on the assumption of ‘‘no rotation’’, and this assumption will be invalid in reality, because the bumpiness of the path could induce camera rotation. (5) Methods based on horizontal strips: Søgaard and Olsen (2003) proposed a crop rows determination by image analysis without segmentation. For a gray-level image after transforming, they divided it into 15 horizontal strips, and then computed the vertical sum of gray values in each strip, the maximum denote the center of crop row in each strip. Lastly, crop rows are detected by the center points. Sainz-Costa, Ribeiro, Burgos-Artizzu, Guijarro, and Pajares (2011) developed a strategy based on analysis of video sequences to detect crop rows. They used the lower half part of the image to detect. The image processing experienced ﬁve steps: segmentation, morphological opening, horizontal strips dividing, vertical average, row centers extracting and crop rows ﬁnding. The above approaches can work well under low weed pressure. However, under the complex conditions such as image with high pressure or serious plant missing, the strip features are usually cannot correctly detect. 1.2. Objectives of the study According to the above mentioned, no previous work considers exploiting the implied information based on geometric property of crop rows. So, from a new point of view, crop rows detection based on multi-ROIs is presented. The overall goal of the present study is to develop an efﬁcient image processing algorithm on the basis of analyzing the virtue of the previous approach for recognizing crop rows. The speciﬁc objectives are as follows: /C15 To develop an image extraction approach for estimating the center points indicating of crop rows, which can work under dif- ferent natural ﬁeld conditions. /C15 To develop a real-time line detection algorithm for crop rows detection. /C15 To evaluate the applicability of the proposed method. 1.3. Introduction to the proposed strategy In this paper, an automatic crop rows detection method is pro- posed. It differs from previous work in that an implicit geometric constraint is employed, which make it possible to well ﬁnd the 2430 G. Jiang et al. / Expert Systems with Applications 42 (2015) 2429–2441 center points of crop rows in a high weed pressure or serious plant deﬁciencies even in the case of no prior knowledge. The ﬂow dia- gram of the proposed method is schematically presented as Fig. 1 , which includes ﬁve steps. In the ﬁrst two steps, i.e., the image graying and binarization, the color indices and Otsu’s method were used to obtain a good segmentation result. After this, in order to extract the candidate center points indicating the crop row centers, a multi-ROIs based on the fact that inter-row space is approximately equal in the ﬁeld was constructed, which fuses the features of multi-rows.

chunks.text: Automatic detection of crop rows based on multi-ROIs Guoquan Jiang, Zhiheng Wang ⇑, Hongmin Liu School of Computer Science and Technology, Henan Polytechnic University, Jiaozuo 454000, PR China article info Article history: Available online 25 October 2014 Keywords: Crop rows detection Multi-ROIs Least squares ﬁtting Precision agriculture Machine vision Autonomous navigation abstract This paper presents a new automatic and robust crop rows detection algorithm for a vision-based agri- cultural machinery guidance system. The algorithm consists of ﬁve steps: gray-level transformation, binarization, candidate center points estimation, real center points conﬁrmation and crop rows detection. During the procedure of candidate points estimation, a multi-ROIs is constructed, which integrates the features of multi-rows based on a geometry constraint that inter-row space is approximately equal into a single processing of optimization. This strategy ensures the center points of crop rows could be detected in a high weedy ﬁeld or in a large barren patch of the ﬁeld. For the fourth step, we used the clustering method to conﬁrm the real center points indicating crop rows. And lastly, the linear regression method was employed to ﬁt the crop rows. Three image data sets, taken from a wheat, corn and soybean under different natural and ﬁeld conditions, were used to evaluate the detection rate, detection accuracy and processing time of the algorithm. Thorough an experimental comparison with the standard Hough trans- form (SHT), it demonstrates the proposed method outperforms SHT either in detection rate, detection accuracy or computation time. The algorithm requires about 61 ms to recognize crop rows for a 640 /C2 480 pixels image while the detection rate reaches 93%, detection accuracy reaches 0.0023 /C176. /C2112014 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction With the development of precision agriculture, the autonomous navigation of agricultural machinery has received more and more attention. It has a wide range of applications, such as automatic spraying pesticide, weeding, harvesting and tilling. The potential advantages of autonomous navigation vehicles may be summa- rized as the following aspects: (1) reduce operator fatigue and improve vehicle positioning accuracy ( Gerrish, Fehr, Van Ee, & Welch, 1997); (2) minimize compaction, leading to improved yield and proﬁtability ( Gan-Mor and Clark, 2001 ); (3) improve efﬁ- ciency; and (4) enhance operation safety ( Han, Zhang, Ni, & Reid, 2004). According to a literature review study ( Billingsley & Schoenﬁsch, 1995; Hague, Marchant, & Tillett, 2000; Li, Imou, Wakabayashi, & Yokoyama, 2009; Mousazadeh, 2013; Wilson, 2000), various guidance technologies, including mechanical guid- ance, optical guidance, radio guidance, Global Positioning System (GPS) and machine vision navigation, etc, have been developed. Especially what deserves to be mentioned is that the vision naviga- tion has already become more and more popular in the agricultural domain, it will largely contribute to the availability of low cost cameras and the plethora of computer vision techniques that could be readily applied ( Hiremath, Van Der Heijden, Van Evert, Stein, & Ter Braak, 2014 ).
